meta-data.title: Multimedia Retrieval HS26
meta-data.description: Exercise questions for MMIR HS26, University Basel

01 - Classical Text Retrieval.question: Document A contains only the words "solar panel efficiency" (3 tokens). Document B discusses solar panel efficiency among many other energy topics (50 tokens, same query terms present). Using cosine similarity for the query "solar panel efficiency", which document scores higher and why?
options: Document B, because it contains more total information about energy and has a richer vector representation
Document A, because the non-query terms in B inflate its vector norm without increasing the dot product
Both score equally because they contain the same query terms with identical frequencies
Document B, because longer documents accumulate more term matches and cosine scales with vector size
01 - Classical Text Retrieval.explanation: Cosine divides by the full vector norm. The non-query terms in B increase ||d|| without contributing to the numerator. This rotates the vector away from the query direction and lowers the score.

01 - Classical Text Retrieval.question: A stemmer reduces both "operating" and "opera" to the same stem "oper". What is the practical consequence for retrieval?
options: Recall improves because grouping related terms increases the number of matching documents
Queries for "opera" return documents about operating systems, producing false positives that hurt precision
Precision improves because a smaller vocabulary reduces the chance of mismatches between queries and documents
The system can no longer distinguish any words that start with the same four letters
01 - Classical Text Retrieval.explanation: Over-stemming merges unrelated words into one token. A search for "opera" now matches documents about "operating", producing false positives that hurt precision rather than improving recall.

01 - Classical Text Retrieval.question: In a retriever-ranker pipeline, what is the role of the retriever?
options: It scores and orders all documents in the collection by their estimated relevance
It quickly selects a candidate set of potentially relevant documents for the ranker
It removes stop words, stems the query, and reformulates it before matching
It presents results to the user with highlighted matches and relevance indicators
01 - Classical Text Retrieval.explanation: The retriever performs fast candidate selection (for example, Boolean OR on query terms). The ranker then scores and orders these candidates by estimated relevance.

01 - Classical Text Retrieval.question: A user searches for "dog forest" and marks two documents as relevant. Both relevant documents contain the word "woodland", while only 2 of the 10 non-relevant documents contain it. In the BIR feedback step, how should the system treat the term "woodland"?
options: Ignore it because it was not part of the original query and only original terms should be scored
Use it as a negative signal to demote documents that contain it alongside the original query terms
Add it to the query with a high positive weight because it separates relevant from non-relevant documents
Replace "forest" with "woodland" in the query since the two words are synonyms in this context
01 - Classical Text Retrieval.explanation: BIR feedback computes weights for all terms, not just query terms. "Woodland" appears in 100% of relevant documents but only 20% of non-relevant documents. This is strong evidence that it helps identify relevant results, so the system should add it to the query with a positive weight.

01 - Classical Text Retrieval.question: A medical reference contains 500 pages covering dozens of conditions. The search system indexes the entire book as a single document. A user searches for "ibuprofen dosage". What is the practical consequence of this granularity choice?
options: The system cannot index the book because it exceeds the maximum allowed document size for the index
The system returns the entire book and the user must locate the relevant page manually
The system returns only the page about ibuprofen because it can identify sub-document sections
The system cannot match the query because the book covers too many unrelated topics at once
01 - Classical Text Retrieval.explanation: Coarse retrieval granularity means the entire book is one retrieval unit. Since the book contains the query terms, it matches, but the system can only return the whole book. The user must then search within it to find the relevant passage. Finer granularity (per section or per page) would let the system point directly to the relevant content.

01 - Classical Text Retrieval.question: A search engine removes all stop words from its index to save storage space. A researcher then searches for the Stephen King novel titled "It". What happens?
options: The query returns zero results because "it" was removed from the index during preprocessing
The query returns every document in the collection because "it" appears everywhere
The system detects that "It" is capitalized and treats it as a proper noun, bypassing stop word removal
Stop word removal only affects the display of results, not matching, so the search works normally
01 - Classical Text Retrieval.explanation: If "it" is on the stop word list, it was stripped from every document during indexing and no longer exists in the vocabulary. When the query arrives, the system cannot find any index entries for this term. This illustrates why aggressive stop word removal can be harmful. The modern approach keeps all terms in the index but assigns low IDF weights to common ones, so they contribute little to ranking without disappearing entirely.

01 - Classical Text Retrieval.question: In the Standard Boolean Model, the query "climate AND biodiversity AND ocean" returns zero results because no single document contains all three terms. Several documents contain two of the three. What does the Extended Boolean Model do differently in this situation?
options: It automatically rewrites the AND query as an OR query so that any matching term produces a result
It assigns graded scores to each term, so partial matches receive positive scores instead of being excluded
It expands the query with synonyms for each term to increase the number of exact matches
It removes the least common query term one at a time until at least one document matches all remaining terms
01 - Classical Text Retrieval.explanation: The Extended Boolean Model replaces the hard true/false evaluation with graded scores between 0 and 1 for each term predicate. The p-norm operators combine these scores so that a document containing two of three query terms receives a positive (though not maximal) score. This produces a ranked list where partial matches appear below exact matches instead of being excluded entirely.

01 - Classical Text Retrieval.question: A company indexes its document collection every night at midnight. During the day, an employee uploads a new report and immediately searches for it. The search returns no results. Why?
options: The report is too short for the system to include in its index and was filtered out automatically
The report was uploaded after the last indexing run and has not yet been added to the search index
New documents must be manually registered by an administrator before the indexer can process them
The system only indexes documents in PDF format and the report was uploaded in a different format
01 - Classical Text Retrieval.explanation: Retrieval is split into an offline indexing phase and an online query phase. The offline phase processes documents into searchable data structures before queries arrive. Documents added between indexing runs do not exist in the index yet and cannot be found, regardless of their content.

01 - Classical Text Retrieval.question: Two news articles are indexed using a bag-of-words representation with stop word removal but no further processing. Article A reports: "Dog bites man". Article B reports: "Man bites dog". A user searches for "dog bites man". How does the retrieval system distinguish between these two articles?
options: TF-IDF weights differ because the terms appear in different syntactic positions within each article
It cannot distinguish them because bag-of-words discards word order, so both articles produce identical vectors
Cosine similarity uses word positions as a secondary signal when comparing documents to the query
The system detects that "bites" has different subjects in each article and creates separate token entries
01 - Classical Text Retrieval.explanation: The bag-of-words model represents each document as a vector of term frequencies. Both articles contain the same three content words ("dog", "bites", "man") with the same frequencies, so they produce identical vectors. The model has no mechanism to capture that the subject and object are swapped. Despite this limitation, bag-of-words works well in practice because term presence and frequency are strong relevance signals for most queries.

01 - Classical Text Retrieval.question: A document collection is indexed without stemming. A user issues the Boolean query "cat AND trees". Document A contains "cat" and "trees". Document B contains "cats" and "tree". Document C contains "feline" and "forest". Which documents does the query return?
options: All three, because they all discuss cats and trees
Only Document A
Documents A and B
Documents A and C
01 - Classical Text Retrieval.explanation: Without stemming, each distinct surface form is an independent token in the vocabulary. "cat" and "cats" have different token IDs and do not match each other. The Boolean predicate requires both exact tokens "cat" and "trees" to be present. Only Document A satisfies this. Stemming would merge "cat"/"cats" and "tree"/"trees" into common stems, and synonym expansion could connect "feline" to "cat", but neither was applied here.

01 - Classical Text Retrieval.question: Two documents are scored with BM25 (k1=1.2, b=0.75) for the query "climate". The collection average document length is 100 tokens. Document M has 50 tokens and mentions "climate" 3 times. Document N has 200 tokens and mentions "climate" 6 times. Document N has twice the raw term frequency. Does it score higher than Document M?
options: Yes, because double the raw occurrences produces roughly double the BM25 relevance score
No, because saturation limits extra repetitions and length normalization penalizes the longer document
They score equally because BM25 normalizes all documents to the same scale before comparing them
Yes, because BM25 always rewards higher raw term frequency regardless of the document's length
01 - Classical Text Retrieval.explanation: BM25 applies two corrections simultaneously. Term-frequency saturation means going from 3 to 6 occurrences adds far less than doubling the score. Document-length normalization penalizes Document N for being twice the average length: its denominator grows because 200/100 = 2.0, making each occurrence worth less. Together, these effects cause the shorter Document M to outscore Document N despite having half the raw term count.

01 - Classical Text Retrieval.question: A Boolean OR query for "cat OR dog OR trees" returns 11 of 12 documents. All returned documents are treated as equally relevant. What fundamental capability does the Vector Space Model add in this situation?
options: It reduces the number of returned documents by applying stricter matching criteria to each candidate
It assigns relevance scores to all 11 documents and ranks them so the strongest matches appear first
It adds the ability to exclude unwanted results using NOT operators on individual query terms
It converts the query into a more precise Boolean expression that filters out weak matches automatically
01 - Classical Text Retrieval.explanation: Boolean retrieval only classifies documents as matching or not matching. The Vector Space Model represents both the query and documents as weighted vectors, then computes a similarity score for each match. Documents sharing more query terms or containing them more frequently score higher. This lets the user focus on the top-ranked results instead of scanning an unordered list of 11 documents.

01 - Classical Text Retrieval.question: A user wants documents about cats but not about the musical "Cats". They write the Boolean query "cat AND NOT musical". The collection contains a document about house cats that mentions "this article appeared in Musical Notes magazine". What happens to this document?
options: It is returned because "cat" is present and "musical" appears in a completely different context
It is excluded because it contains the token "musical" and Boolean NOT cannot distinguish word meanings
It is returned with a lower relevance score because "musical" is present but used in a non-theatrical context
The system detects that "musical" refers to a magazine name and keeps the document in the results
01 - Classical Text Retrieval.explanation: Boolean NOT checks only whether the token is present, not what it means. Since the document contains "musical" (from the magazine name), the NOT predicate evaluates to false and the entire expression fails. The Standard Boolean Model has no mechanism to distinguish between the theatrical sense and the incidental use of the same word.

01 - Classical Text Retrieval.question: A search system normalizes all document vectors to unit length during indexing and stores only these unit vectors. At query time, it computes the raw inner product between the unnormalized query vector and each stored unit vector. A colleague argues this is wrong because "cosine similarity divides by both norms, not just the document norm". Is the colleague right?
options: Yes, omitting the query norm produces a fundamentally different ranking than true cosine similarity
No, the query norm is a constant for all documents in the same query and does not change the ranking order
Yes, both the query and document vectors must be unit length for the inner product to equal cosine
No, normalizing the document vectors to unit length implicitly normalizes the query vector as well
01 - Classical Text Retrieval.explanation: Full cosine similarity divides the dot product by both norms. Pre-normalizing documents means the system computes dot(q, d/||d||) = dot(q,d)/||d||, which differs from cosine by the missing factor 1/||q||. But for a given query, ||q|| is the same constant for every document comparison. Dividing all scores by the same constant preserves ranking order. This optimization lets systems avoid recomputing document norms at query time.

01 - Classical Text Retrieval.question: In the original BM25 IDF formula, the weight depends on the ratio of documents that do not contain a term to those that do. A collection has 10,000 documents and a term appears in 8,000 of them. What happens to this term's IDF weight?
options: It receives a large positive weight because the term is well-represented
It becomes negative, so a matching term would lower a document's score
It becomes exactly zero, contributing nothing to the score
The formula is undefined for terms with document frequency above N/2
01 - Classical Text Retrieval.explanation: Substituting into the BM25 IDF formula gives log((10000 - 8000 + 0.5) / (8000 + 0.5)) = log(2000.5 / 8000.5), which is approximately -0.60. A negative IDF means that finding this very common term in a document actively lowers its score. This is why many implementations (including Lucene) use an always-positive IDF variant instead.

01 - Classical Text Retrieval.question: A company splits every email into individual sentences and indexes each sentence as a separate document. A user searches for "project deadline moved to Friday". The relevant email discusses this change across three consecutive sentences: one mentions the project, another mentions the deadline, and a third mentions Friday. What problem does this granularity choice create?
options: The system returns too many short results because sentence-level documents match partial queries very easily
No single sentence contains all query terms, so the relevant information is split across retrieval units
Sentence-level indexing requires far more storage than document-level and makes query processing slower
The system cannot assign meaningful term weights to individual sentences because they contain too few words
01 - Classical Text Retrieval.explanation: Overly fine granularity splits coherent content across multiple retrieval units. Each sentence is scored independently, and none contains all query terms. The system may return some sentences with low partial-match scores, but it has no mechanism to recognize that three adjacent sentences together answer the query. This is the opposite problem of too-coarse granularity, where the returned unit is too large to be useful.

01 - Classical Text Retrieval.question: A user searches for "went hiking" in two systems. System A uses Porter stemming. System B uses lemmatization. The collection contains documents with "go hiking" and "goes for hikes". Which system finds more of these documents, and why?
options: System A, because stemming applies more aggressive reduction rules than lemmatization for all word forms
System B, because it maps "went" to "go" using a dictionary; stemming cannot reduce irregular forms
Both find identical results because "went" and "go" share a common stem after suffix stripping
Neither system matches "went" to "go" because the two words share no common surface-level pattern
01 - Classical Text Retrieval.explanation: Porter stemming applies rule-based suffix stripping. "Went" has no suffix to strip, so it stays "went" and never matches "go" or "goes". This is under-stemming: the failure to merge irregular forms. Lemmatization uses a dictionary to map "went" to its lemma "go", successfully connecting it to documents containing "go" and "goes". The trade-off is that lemmatization requires language-specific resources and is computationally more expensive.

01 - Classical Text Retrieval.question: A user searches a Boolean system for "(cat AND dog) OR hound". The collection is indexed without stemming. Document A contains "cat" and "hound". Document B contains "dog" and "hound". Document C contains "cat" and "dog". Document D contains only "hound". Which documents are returned?
options: Only Document C, because it is the only one satisfying the AND clause
Documents C and D only
Documents A, B, C, and D
Documents A and B only
01 - Classical Text Retrieval.explanation: The OR operator requires only one side to be true. Document C satisfies the left side (cat AND dog). Documents A, B, and D each contain "hound", satisfying the right side. The trap is focusing only on the AND clause and forgetting that any document matching the OR alternative also qualifies.

01 - Classical Text Retrieval.question: A user searches the Vector Space Model for "network network security" (the term "network" typed twice). Compared to searching for "network security" (each term once), how does the repeated term affect the inner product ranking?
options: No effect; the VSM removes duplicate terms from the query vector before scoring any documents
It doubles the query weight for "network", so documents strong in that term get a larger boost
It reduces the weight for "network" because the system penalizes repeated terms in the query
It triggers phrase matching and searches for the literal string "network network security"
01 - Classical Text Retrieval.explanation: The query is processed through the same TF-IDF pipeline as documents. "Network" appears twice, so its query-vector component is 2 * idf(network), while "security" has 1 * idf(security). The inner product multiplies each document term weight by the corresponding query weight, so documents rich in "network" gain more than documents rich only in "security". This effectively lets users emphasize specific terms by repeating them.

01 - Classical Text Retrieval.question: In BM25, the parameter k1 controls how quickly the term-frequency component saturates. Higher k1 values let additional occurrences of a term contribute more before the ceiling is reached. What does setting k1 = 0 effectively turn BM25 into?
options: A model equivalent to raw TF-IDF with no saturation
A binary model where only term presence matters, ignoring repetition count
A model that ranks all documents equally regardless of content
A model equivalent to cosine similarity with length normalization
01 - Classical Text Retrieval.explanation: With k1 = 0, the function becomes tf * 1 / (tf + 0) = 1 for any positive tf. Whether a term appears once or a thousand times, its contribution is the same. Combined with IDF, this produces a weighted set-of-words model: each query term present in the document contributes its IDF weight exactly once, regardless of frequency.

02 - Performance Evaluation.question: A benchmark deliberately separates the "information need" from the "query". Why does this distinction matter when assessors label documents?
options: Assessors judge documents against the underlying need, so the need must be written unambiguously
The literal query keywords are used for judging, while the need is shown only to users
Queries must be frozen for reproducibility, whereas the need may change over time
The separation matters for ranked retrieval but not for set-based retrieval
02 - Performance Evaluation.explanation: Relevance is judged against what the user actually wants, not the keywords they happen to type. Two assessors must interpret the need the same way, which is only possible if the need is written out clearly. Vague needs produce inconsistent labels that no metric can repair.

02 - Performance Evaluation.question: An evaluation pools true positives and false negatives across all 40 needs before computing a single recall figure. One need contains more relevant documents than the other 39 combined. What does the resulting recall value mainly reflect?
options: The dominant need alone, because it supplies most of the counts that go into the pool
An equal blend of all needs, because pooling gives every need the same weight
The 39 smaller needs, because together they outnumber the single large one
Only the needs on which the system found no relevant documents
02 - Performance Evaluation.explanation: Pooling counts before dividing (micro-averaging) weights every document equally, so a need that supplies most of the relevant documents dominates the result. The many small needs barely register. This is why retrieval evaluation usually prefers macro-averaging, where each need contributes equally regardless of its size.

02 - Performance Evaluation.question: A search task typically returns many relevant documents per query, and the user wants all of them, not just the first. An engineer summarises ranking quality with mean reciprocal rank. Why is this the wrong tool here?
options: Reciprocal rank cannot be averaged across a set of multiple queries
It reflects only the first relevant result and ignores all relevant documents below it
It needs graded relevance judgments that this particular task does not provide
It actively penalises any system that returns more than one relevant document
02 - Performance Evaluation.explanation: Reciprocal rank only measures how far down the first relevant result sits. A system that places five relevant documents at the top scores the same as one that places a single relevant document there and nothing else. When many relevant documents matter, a measure that values the whole ranking, such as average precision, is the right choice.

02 - Performance Evaluation.question: A metric adds up the relevance grades of the documents in the top k positions, ignoring their order within that window. Which existing measure is it best understood as a refinement of?
options: Precision at k, refined to weight each result by its degree of relevance
Recall at k, refined to weight each result by its degree of relevance
Discounted cumulative gain, simplified to run faster by dropping the discount
Reciprocal rank, extended to look beyond just the first relevant result
02 - Performance Evaluation.explanation: Cumulative gain counts the relevant material sitting in the top k, just as precision at k does, but instead of treating every relevant item alike it weights each by its grade. So it reads as a graded refinement of precision at k. It is not recall, which divides by the total relevant in the collection. And dropping the discount from DCG is not an efficiency trick: it removes position sensitivity, giving a different measure rather than a faster one.

02 - Performance Evaluation.question: A classifier is evaluated on a dataset where only 2% of items belong to the positive class, and it reports 96% accuracy. Why can this number be misleading?
options: Accuracy simply cannot be computed when the two classes are heavily imbalanced
A model that always predicts the majority class could match it while finding no positives
High accuracy on imbalanced data guarantees high precision on the positive class
Accuracy overweights the rare positive class here, which artificially inflates the score
02 - Performance Evaluation.explanation: When one class dominates, accuracy is driven by the majority. A trivial model that always predicts the majority class would score close to 98% here while never detecting a single positive item. Accuracy hides this failure, so precision, recall, and specificity must be reported separately on imbalanced data.

02 - Performance Evaluation.question: A biometric unlock system must almost never accept an impostor, though occasionally rejecting the real owner is tolerable. When picking an operating point on the ROC curve, which properties should the designers prioritise?
options: A low false-positive rate and high positive predictive value on accepted attempts
A high true-positive rate, accepting more impostors as an unavoidable cost
The threshold that maximises overall accuracy across all unlock attempts
A high true-negative rate paired with a deliberately high false-positive rate
02 - Performance Evaluation.explanation: A false positive here is a security breach, so the system needs a very low false-positive rate: it should hardly ever accept the wrong person. It also wants high positive predictive value, so that an accepted face is almost certainly the owner. Maximising accuracy or the true-positive rate would let more impostors through, which is exactly the error this application cannot afford.

02 - Performance Evaluation.question: A new retrieval algorithm is tested on a reused benchmark whose relevance judgments were built years earlier by pooling other systems' results. The new algorithm surfaces useful documents no earlier system had found. How does the score treat them?
options: They raise the score, since finding any relevant document improves recall
They count as non-relevant, so the system is penalised for finding new material
They are automatically sent for fresh judging before the final score is computed
They are excluded and change neither precision nor recall in any direction
02 - Performance Evaluation.explanation: Pooling judges only the documents that participating systems retrieved and treats everything unjudged as not relevant. A later system that finds genuinely relevant documents outside that pool gets no credit for them; they score as misses. The novel system is penalised for its originality, which is a systematic bias of reused benchmarks.

02 - Performance Evaluation.question: One team reports that system P beats system Q on mean average precision, while another reports that Q beats P on nDCG at rank 10. Both numbers are computed correctly. What is the most likely explanation?
options: One team made an arithmetic mistake, because the two metrics must always agree
P finds more relevant documents overall, while Q fills the very top of the list
The two metrics measure the same property, so the disagreement is only random noise
Q used graded relevance and P used binary, so the comparison is not valid
02 - Performance Evaluation.explanation: Mean average precision integrates precision over the full result list and heavily penalises missed relevant documents, so it rewards a system that finds more of them. nDCG at rank 10 evaluates only a short window and rewards packing high-value documents near the very top, ignoring what lies beyond the cutoff. The two measures answer different questions, so a system can win on one and lose on the other.

02 - Performance Evaluation.question: A spam filter is tuned on a balanced test set and reports high precision. It is then deployed on real mail, where spam is only a small fraction of messages. Its recall and specificity are unchanged, yet users complain that many flagged messages are actually legitimate. What happened?
options: The same specificity now flags a fixed share of a much larger legitimate pool
Recall fell in deployment, so far more spam now slips past into the inbox
The decision threshold shifted on its own when the filter reached production
Deployment raised the overall accuracy, which forces precision down in exchange
02 - Performance Evaluation.explanation: Precision depends on class balance; recall and specificity do not. Specificity is a rate over the negatives, so when legitimate mail vastly outnumbers spam, that fixed rate produces many false positives in absolute terms, and they come to outnumber the true positives. Precision drops even though the classifier is unchanged. This is the test-versus-production prevalence mismatch: a benchmark whose class balance differs from deployment reports a precision the live system will not reproduce.

02 - Performance Evaluation.question: A compliance team wants one number to compare two filters on an unordered result set. For them, missing a relevant document is about four times as costly as returning an irrelevant one, and they want that priority built into the score. Which metric fits?
options: Precision
F-score
Recall
Fallout
02 - Performance Evaluation.explanation: The team wants a single number that combines precision and recall for an unordered set, with recall weighted more heavily because misses are costlier. The F-score does this, and its beta parameter lets the weighting favour recall. Precision or recall alone captures only one side, and fallout measures irrelevant intake rather than a balance of the two.

02 - Performance Evaluation.question: An evaluation spans many needs, and the number of relevant documents varies widely from one need to the next. The team wants a single-point precision summary per need whose cutoff adjusts automatically to how many relevant documents that need has. Which metric fits?
options: Precision at 10
Average precision
R-precision
Fallout
02 - Performance Evaluation.explanation: The team wants one precision value per need at a cutoff that matches how many relevant documents the need has. R-precision evaluates precision after exactly R documents, where R is the number of relevant documents, so its cutoff self-adjusts. Precision at 10 fixes the cutoff regardless of the need; average precision summarises the full curve rather than one point; fallout measures irrelevant intake.

02 - Performance Evaluation.question: A vendor advertises that its search engine is 40% more accurate than a rival, but does not say which document collection was used, which queries were run, who judged the results, or what "accurate" means. Beyond the missing details, what is the fundamental reason this claim carries little weight?
options: Accuracy is never a valid measure for comparing two search systems
It cannot be reproduced or independently challenged by anyone else
A gain of 40% is too large to be plausible for a real engine
It would be valid had the vendor reported precision and recall
02 - Performance Evaluation.explanation: A scientific comparison fixes the collection, the queries, the judgments, and the measure in advance, so anyone can rerun it and get the same numbers. A claim that names none of these cannot be checked or contested, and it is easy to manufacture by selecting the queries where your system happens to win. The problem is not the size of the number or the choice of measure, but that it is not reproducible.

02 - Performance Evaluation.question: In a two-stage pipeline, an early retriever selects candidate documents and a later ranker reorders them for the user. The designers tune the retriever to favour recall, even though this lets in many irrelevant candidates. Why is this the right choice?
options: The ranker needs irrelevant documents present in order to score at all
Recall matters more than precision in every possible retrieval setting
A dropped relevant document can never be recovered by the ranker
More candidates make the ranker run faster on the same query
02 - Performance Evaluation.explanation: The ranker can only reorder documents the retriever passed forward, so a relevant document missed at the first stage is lost for good. An irrelevant candidate, by contrast, can still be pushed down or removed by the ranker. This asymmetry is why the retriever is optimized for recall and the ranker for precision, and it is specific to this pipeline rather than a universal rule that recall beats precision.

02 - Performance Evaluation.question: A system returns a short, very clean ranking: the few documents it retrieves are almost all relevant and sit at the very top, but it misses most of the relevant documents in the collection. Its average precision comes out surprisingly low. Why?
options: Average precision divides by every relevant document, so misses count as zeros
Average precision only rewards long lists and caps short rankings low
Average precision skips the top positions and averages the lower ranks
Average precision counts each irrelevant document twice, halving the score
02 - Performance Evaluation.explanation: Average precision sums the precision at each rank where a relevant document appears, then divides by the total number of relevant documents in the collection, not by the number found. A document that is never retrieved contributes nothing to the sum but is still counted in the denominator, acting as an implicit zero. A system that finds only a few of many relevant documents therefore scores low, however clean its short list is.

02 - Performance Evaluation.question: A team computes discounted cumulative gain at rank 10 for each query and notices the raw values swing wildly between queries, even for a system that behaves consistently. They switch to the normalized version. What problem does normalization solve?
options: The discount factor only becomes correct after dividing by the rank
Raw discounted gain ignores position, and normalization restores it
Normalization removes the need to assign graded relevance judgments
Different queries have different relevant counts and grades, so raw scores differ
02 - Performance Evaluation.explanation: Raw discounted cumulative gain depends on how many relevant documents a query has and how high their grades are, so a query with several high-grade documents can score far above another regardless of system quality. Normalizing by the ideal ranking's gain places every query on a 0-to-1 scale, making scores comparable and averageable across queries. Discounting already handles position, and normalization does not remove the need for graded judgments.

02 - Performance Evaluation.question: An intent router handles four categories. One is rare but critical: misrouting it produces a confidently wrong answer. Overall accuracy is high, yet the team suspects the rare category performs badly. Which summary would expose this, and why?
options: Accuracy at a higher threshold recounts the rare category more fairly
Macro averaging weights every category equally, regardless of its size
Micro-averaged precision gives the rare category more pooled influence
The largest category's false-positive rate dominates the overall total
02 - Performance Evaluation.explanation: Accuracy and micro-averaging weight each item equally, so the common categories dominate and a rare category's failure is invisible. Macro-averaging computes the metric per category and then averages, giving the rare category the same weight as the common ones. Its poor recall then pulls the macro score down, exposing the failure that accuracy hides.

02 - Performance Evaluation.question: An engineer sweeps a classifier's decision threshold to find the value that gives the best results, then reports that same value's performance as the system's final score. A reviewer objects. What is the flaw?
options: A threshold should never change once the classifier is trained
Sweeping the threshold alters the classifier's underlying score distribution
The score was tuned and reported on the very same data
The best threshold can only be found by maximising accuracy
02 - Performance Evaluation.explanation: Choosing the threshold to maximise performance on a dataset and then reporting performance on that same dataset optimises against the answers, which inflates the score. Threshold selection must happen on a separate validation set, with the test set used only once for the final report. Sweeping the threshold changes only the decision boundary, not the underlying scores, and any metric can guide the choice.

02 - Performance Evaluation.question: Across 50 needs, system X reaches a mean average precision of 0.42 and system Y reaches 0.41. Per-need scores for both systems range from near zero to above 0.8. Before claiming X is better, what should the analyst check?
options: Whether X retrieved more documents in total than Y overall
Whether the gap would grow with more relevant documents per need
Whether the two systems used different relevance judgment scales
Whether the gap survives a paired significance test across the needs
02 - Performance Evaluation.explanation: Per-need scores vary enormously, so a one-point difference in the mean can easily be swamped by that spread. A paired significance test on the per-need average precision values, such as a paired t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank test, checks whether the difference is consistent across needs rather than the product of a few easy or hard queries. Total documents retrieved, denser judgments, or the grading scale do not settle whether the mean gap is real.

02 - Performance Evaluation.question: A system retrieves almost every relevant document for each query, so its recall is excellent. Yet users on the results page complain they cannot find anything useful near the top. Which measure would reveal the problem that recall hides?
options: Fallout, the count of irrelevant documents in the whole collection
Precision at the first few ranks, where users actually look
Recall at a larger cutoff, confirming the documents were retrieved
The total number of documents the system retrieved per query
02 - Performance Evaluation.explanation: Recall counts whether relevant documents were found anywhere in the list; it says nothing about where they sit. If they are buried below many irrelevant results, users reading from the top never reach them. Precision at the first few ranks measures exactly the region users inspect, exposing the poor ordering that high recall conceals. Fallout, deeper recall, and result-set size do not describe the top of the list.

02 - Performance Evaluation.question: A large language model scores very high on a public multiple-choice exam benchmark. Before treating this as evidence of reasoning ability, what should you consider?
options: Multiple-choice benchmarks cannot measure a model's ability at all
A high benchmark score always proves genuine generalisation
The model must have tuned its answers on a validation split
The questions and answers may have been in the training data
02 - Performance Evaluation.explanation: Models trained on web-scale text may have seen public exam questions and their answers during training. A high score can then reflect memorisation of the answers rather than reasoning about the task. This is benchmark contamination, and it means the score is not evidence of generalisation to unseen problems.

03 - Advanced Text Processing.question: A search system folds every accent to its base letter before indexing. For a collection in a single European language where an accented spelling and its unaccented spelling can be two different words, what is the main consequence?
options: Precision drops, because distinct words collapse into one token
Recall drops, because accented documents stop matching accented queries
The index grows, because each word stores several accented variants
Latency rises, because every token needs Unicode normalization
03 - Advanced Text Processing.explanation: Folding maps different words that differ only by an accent onto the same token, so a query for one retrieves documents about the other. That is a precision loss; recall is unaffected or slightly helped. The trade is recall gained for precision lost.

03 - Advanced Text Processing.question: A film's title consists entirely of common function words. What happens if the pipeline strips stop words before indexing the title?
options: The title becomes empty and cannot be found by title
The title is indexed under its first content-bearing word
The title survives intact, because titles skip stop-word removal
The title matches nearly every document in the collection
03 - Advanced Text Processing.explanation: Stop-word removal deletes high-frequency function words. A title built only from those words leaves nothing behind, so the exact phrase becomes unsearchable. This is why stop words must not be stripped from phrase or title queries.

03 - Advanced Text Processing.question: On a large corpus, two adjacent words each occur thousands of times and nearly always appear together as a well-known company name. One collocation measure ranks the pair near the top, another buries it far down. Which behaviour belongs to which measure?
options: Likelihood ratio ranks it high; pointwise mutual information ranks it low
Pointwise mutual information ranks it high; likelihood ratio ranks it low
Both measures rank the pair near the top
Both measures push the pair far down
03 - Advanced Text Processing.explanation: The likelihood ratio measures evidence for dependence, which grows with frequency, so a frequent tight pair sits at the top. Pointwise mutual information measures association strength relative to how common each word is, so common words drag its score down even for a genuine pair. The two fail in opposite directions.

03 - Advanced Text Processing.question: A one-word query is submitted that has several unrelated meanings, with no other words attached. The system uses classical, context-based sense disambiguation. What is the realistic outcome?
options: Neither classical technique resolves it from the query alone
Part-of-speech tagging picks the correct sense on its own
Restoring the surrounding stop words fixes the sense
A synonym list expands the query to its most frequent sense
03 - Advanced Text Processing.explanation: Classical sense disambiguation reads the words around the ambiguous term. A bare one-word query supplies none, so the sense cannot be fixed from the query itself. The standard response is to return results for both senses or offer a 'did you mean' prompt. Genuine ambiguity with no context is inherent to language and no classical technique removes it.

03 - Advanced Text Processing.question: A team trains a Naive Bayes intent router on past query logs, where most historical traffic went to general web search, and uses the empirical class prior from that data. What goes wrong?
options: New queries are routed to web search almost regardless of their features
Rare intents can never be assigned to any query
Training fails, because the class counts are imbalanced
The router stays accurate but grows slow on the rarer intents
03 - Advanced Text Processing.explanation: The prior term encodes each class's base rate. When one class dominates the logs, its large prior swamps the feature evidence, so almost everything is routed there. The fix is a uniform prior, or balancing the training data before estimating priors.

03 - Advanced Text Processing.question: A pipeline detects language with a few hand-written rules (script, diacritics, function-word counts). It works well on full documents but fails on very short queries. What is the standard fix?
options: Replace the rules with a classifier over character n-grams
Add more hand-written rules until short queries are covered
Match the query against a dictionary of every word per language
Skip detection for short queries and run every language pipeline
03 - Advanced Text Processing.explanation: Hand rules need several signals to fire, which long text provides but short queries do not. A character n-gram classifier weighs whatever partial evidence exists and returns the most probable language with a confidence score, so it degrades gracefully on short input instead of failing outright.

03 - Advanced Text Processing.question: Across phrase indexing, compound splitting, and spelling correction, the same choice recurs: store the original token and also add the derived tokens (the phrase, the parts, or the corrected form) instead of replacing the original. What does this choice protect, and at what cost?
options: It protects recall, at the cost of index size and some precision
It protects precision, at the cost of lower recall
It protects ranking quality, at the cost of slower queries
It protects storage, at the cost of missing partial matches
03 - Advanced Text Processing.explanation: Keeping the original alongside the derived tokens lets a query match through any of them, an over-indexing strategy that preserves recall. The price is a larger index and some incidental matches that lower precision. The same pattern appears wherever the pipeline adds tokens rather than rewriting in place.

03 - Advanced Text Processing.question: A team switches to a very aggressive stemmer that reduces words to short stems. Two unrelated words now share the same stem. What is the practical consequence for retrieval?
options: Precision drops, as documents about one word match queries for the other
Recall drops, as the two words no longer share an index entry
Query latency rises, as the stemmer runs more rule scans
The index grows, as each word stores several candidate stems
03 - Advanced Text Processing.explanation: Over-stemming collapses distinct words onto one token, so a query for one retrieves documents about the other. That is a precision loss. Aggressive stemmers trade precision for speed and higher recall, acceptable only when collisions rarely affect ranking.

03 - Advanced Text Processing.question: A decompounder splits every compound into its parts and indexes those parts. It processes a compound whose meaning is not the sum of its parts (a term that is not actually a kind of the thing its last part names). What is the risk?
options: Precision drops, as the wrong-sense parts match unrelated queries
Recall drops, as the full compound is removed from the index
The compound can no longer be found by its exact spelling
Query latency rises, as every compound is split at search time
03 - Advanced Text Processing.explanation: Endocentric compounds (a bookcase is a kind of case) split safely. Exocentric compounds do not: splitting adds parts with the wrong meaning, so the document matches queries about those parts and precision falls. Whether to split depends on the collection.

03 - Advanced Text Processing.question: A spell-checker rewrites every variant spelling of a personal name to one canonical form, at both index and query time. Why is this risky for name search?
options: Distinct people can be merged into one and some become unfindable
Recall drops, as the canonical spelling matches fewer documents
The name can no longer be found under its original spelling
Query latency rises, as every name triggers a phonetic lookup
03 - Advanced Text Processing.explanation: A single canonical rewrite treats every variant as a typo of one name. But some variants are themselves other people's genuine names, so those people get folded into the wrong identity and become unfindable. The safer approach keeps the original spelling and expands to variants at query time rather than rewriting.

03 - Advanced Text Processing.question: An intent router should treat 'contains a person entity together with a leading WH-word' as a combined signal that means more than either feature alone. Why does a Naive Bayes classifier handle this poorly?
options: It scores each feature independently and cannot represent their combination
It drops one of the two features to keep the feature space small
It requires the two features to be perfectly correlated in training
It treats WH-words as stop words and removes them before scoring
03 - Advanced Text Processing.explanation: Naive Bayes assumes features are conditionally independent given the class, so it multiplies per-feature likelihoods and cannot express that two features together carry extra signal. Conjunctions like this are why production routers move to a small neural classifier that models feature interactions.

03 - Advanced Text Processing.question: In the query pipeline, named entity recognition runs before intent classification. What breaks if these two steps are swapped?
options: The classifier loses the entity-type features it depends on
The entity recognizer loses the language label it depends on
Both steps produce the same result, so the order does not matter
Spell correction can no longer run on the extracted entities
03 - Advanced Text Processing.explanation: Intent classification uses entity types (has-PERSON, has-DATE, has-LOCATION) as input features. If classification runs first, those features do not exist yet, so the router decides on weaker signals. This is why NER precedes intent classification in the pipeline.

03 - Advanced Text Processing.question: A system indexes text as overlapping character trigrams instead of whole words. A query arrives with a small typo and a different word ending. What does this representation make possible?
options: Most trigrams still match, so partial matching retrieves the passage
Every trigram must match, so the typo blocks all retrieval
The typo is corrected automatically before any trigrams are formed
Only the unchanged suffix trigrams are used for matching
03 - Advanced Text Processing.explanation: Shingling text into overlapping trigrams means a typo or an inflected ending changes only a few trigrams, leaving most shared between query and document. A retrieval model that supports partial matching then finds the passage without an explicit spell-checker or stemmer.

03 - Advanced Text Processing.question: A dictionary lemmatizer is given a word that can be either a noun or a verb, but it receives the wrong part-of-speech tag. What is the effect?
options: It returns the wrong base form, because the lemma depends on the tag
It returns the token unchanged, because the tag is ignored
It returns both possible base forms and lets the ranker choose
It raises an error, because the tag does not match the word
03 - Advanced Text Processing.explanation: A lemmatizer uses the part-of-speech tag to pick the right base form; the noun and verb readings of one surface form have different lemmas. A wrong tag therefore yields the wrong lemma, which is why accurate POS tagging must precede lemmatization.

03 - Advanced Text Processing.question: In a specialist search domain, users type a short community term while the documents use a completely different full name for the same thing. A general-purpose thesaurus does not link them. What restores recall?
options: A hand-maintained domain synonym list mapping the term to the full name
A stemmer configured for the domain's most frequent language
A stop-word list extended with the community term
A phonetic code shared by the term and the full name
03 - Advanced Text Processing.explanation: General thesauri cover linguistic synonyms, not domain shorthand, so they miss the mapping. A synonym list maintained by the search team links the community term to the document term, and query expansion then reaches documents that never use the typed term. Dense embeddings are the modern alternative for the long tail.

03 - Advanced Text Processing.question: A pipeline already applies stemming and lemmatization to every token. Why does it still need separate phrase detection and compound splitting?
options: Stemming and lemmatization act only on single words, not multi-word or in-token meaning
Stemming and lemmatization lower recall, which phrases and compounds restore
Phrase and compound steps replace stemming for languages without inflection
Phrase and compound steps run only when no stop-word list is available
03 - Advanced Text Processing.explanation: Stemming and lemmatization decide which single-word forms are equivalent. They cannot join 'New York' into one concept or split a compound into its parts, because those cases involve meaning across or inside token boundaries. Phrase detection and compound splitting handle exactly that.

03 - Advanced Text Processing.question: A code-search index stores each multi-word identifier (written in camelCase or with underscores) as a single token. A user searches for one of the words inside such an identifier. What happens?
options: The search misses it, because the sub-word is not a token on its own
The search finds it, because identifiers are split on case changes by default
The search finds it, because underscores are always treated as spaces
The search misses it, because identifiers are dropped as stop words
03 - Advanced Text Processing.explanation: Storing an identifier whole means its component words are not separate tokens, so a query for one of them cannot match. Splitting identifiers on case changes and underscores at index time adds the sub-words and fixes this.

03 - Advanced Text Processing.question: A two-word place name is made of two otherwise common words. Under a plain bag-of-words index, a search for the name also retrieves documents where the two words appear unrelated. What restores precision?
options: Indexing the two words together as a single phrase token
Dropping the more common of the two words as a stop word
Stemming both words to their shortest common form
Lowering the weight of both words in the ranking
03 - Advanced Text Processing.explanation: A bag-of-words index cannot tell a genuine name from an incidental co-occurrence of its two words. Adding the pair as one phrase token gives the ranker a clean signal that the words appeared together, which raises precision without hurting recall.

03 - Advanced Text Processing.question: A team can route every query with a single large-language-model call that extracts entities, detects language, and classifies intent. Why do production stacks still run the classical pipeline first and use the model only for hard cases?
options: The classical pipeline is far cheaper and faster per query, so it handles the bulk
The model cannot detect language, so the classical step must do it
The model cannot output structured fields, so the classical step is required
The classical pipeline is more accurate on every query than the model
03 - Advanced Text Processing.explanation: A model call costs measurable money and adds hundreds of milliseconds, while the classical stack runs in well under a millisecond at no per-query cost and returns calibrated confidences. Stacks therefore run the classical pipeline on all traffic and escalate to the model only where confidence is low or the value is high.

03 - Advanced Text Processing.question: Besides labelling entities, how does named entity recognition help the phrase-indexing step?
options: It proposes multi-word entities as ready-made phrases to index as units
It removes entity words from the phrase candidates to save space
It replaces the frequency filters used to score candidate phrases
It lowers the weight of entity phrases so common words rank higher
03 - Advanced Text Processing.explanation: When the recognizer marks several words as one entity, such as a person or a place, those words already form a phrase. The pipeline can index that phrase as a unit straight away. This is faster and more targeted than scoring every word pair in the corpus, because named entities are the phrases that entity search cares about.
